newsitem.title: USA: Interned Japanese-Americans get diplomas 50 years on.
newsitem.headline: Interned Japanese-Americans get diplomas 50 years on.

text.p: Sixty-six Americans of Japanese descent proudly accepted high school diplomas on Tuesday more than 50 years after their studies were interrupted by internment during the Second World War.

As teenagers, the former San Francisco high school students were among about 120,000 Japanese-Americans that the U.S. government sent to internment camps during the war, denying them their San Francisco school diplomas.
The city tried to make amends on Tuesday, holding a special graduation ceremony to award them the diplomas they would have received if they had been allowed to finish high school.

Sixty-six Japanese-Americans from the graduating classes of 1942 through 1945, many frail or white-haired now, smiled proudly as they accepted their diplomas from city officials at the ceremony at the civic auditorium.
The graduating students, who came from many parts of the United States and from as far afield as Japan for the ceremony, were applauded by hundreds of present-day students in the audience.

San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown said it was a "terrible time" when President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on February 19, 1942, which ordered the internment of Japanese-Americans in the Western United States in camps.
It was an even worse time when the order was implemented "without a whisper by many other Americans," he said.

"How can that ever be undone? I would guess that it cannot be undone," he said. But it should serve as a lesson so that "never again will any of us even come close to remaining silent or inactive in case any improper conduct is attempted ...by our government," Brown said.
The San Francisco Board of Education passed a resolution last November calling for school officials to find Japanese-Americans who were forced to interrupt their high school education by internment.
One graduating student, Koji Ozawa, who should have graduated from San Francisco's Lowell High School in 1944, said he felt very proud to belatedly receive the diploma.

"I had a sister and a brother who are graduates of Lowell High School. Then in the 1970s my three children graduated from Lowell High School. Now finally I got a diploma showing that I'm a graduate of Lowell High School. It completes a cycle, so I feel very good about it," he said.
The ceremony was "sort of an atonement for what happened in those days. Besides, you get to meet all these friends that I haven't seen for a long time," Ozawa said.

Ozawa, a 70-year-old retired civil engineer, said his family was sent to an internment camp in the spring of 1942. First they were sent to Tanforan race track near San Francisco where families lived in converted stables.

Then they were sent to a permanent camp in Utah called Topaz, where life was harsh, he said. "We all lived in one room, a family of five. We had to go outside to take a shower, go outside to eat. In the winter it was very cold, in the summer it was very dusty," he said.
The evacuees went to makeshift schools in the internment camps and were awarded diplomas from the camp high schools.

Masaru Kawaguchi, a 71-year-old retired engineer who received his diploma from San Francisco's Washington High School on Tuesday, helped track down the internees using school year books and other records.

He said more than 130 people would have been eligible for the diplomas, but some did not want to come to the ceremony. "They want nothing to do with that. They want to forget all about these memories of internment camps," he said.
